newsitem.title: FRANCE: Nazis jailed for desecrating French Jewish tombs.
newsitem.headline: Nazis jailed for desecrating French Jewish tombs.

text.p: A court jailed four neo-Nazis on Thursday for desecrating a Jewish cemetery in southern France in 1990 in an attack that caused worldwide revulsion.

The Marseille court sentenced non-commissioned army officer Olivier Fimbry and Patrick Laonegro, described as the ideologist of the group, to two years in prison -- the maximum term -- on charges of desecrating the cemetery in the southern town of Carpentras.

The other two defendants, Yannick Garnier and Bertrand Nouveau, who had expressed most remorse, received 20-month sentences. The four will also have to pay total compensation of around 125,000 francs ($21,500).

The attack on the centuries-old graveyard, in which the recently buried body of Felix Germon was disinterred and his sodomisation simulated with a beach umbrella, provoked disgust throughout France and the world.
Thirty-four graves were wrecked in the attack, which the then Socialist government blamed on the ideology of extreme-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen.
Outrage sent hundreds of thousands of people into the streets in a protest march led by late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.

Garnier's confession last July led to the arrest of his accomplices six years after the attack. All four defendants, in their late 20s or early 30s, expressed remorse for the desecration in court last month.
But Fimbry and Laonegro said they still admired Nazi ideology while Garnier and Nouveau asked for forgiveness from the Jewish community and Germon's widow Magdeleine.

The four will have to pay Magdeleine Germon 50,000 francs ($8,600) compensation, just over 27,000 francs ($4,650) to the Carpentras municipality and about 5,000 francs ($860) each to about 10 civil plaintiffs including relatives of the dead and anti-racism groups.
Magdeleine Germon's lawyer, Jean-Marc Fedida, said he was "disappointed by a judgement that values Madame Germon's six years of suffering at 50,000 francs."
But Alain Lhote, a lawyer for civil plaintiffs including anti-racism groups, said they were satisfied by the ruling as a warning to anyone tempted to carry out racist outrages.
At the trial last month, lawyers for anti-racist groups accused Le Pen of whipping up anti-Semitism in France.
Le Pen, who has long campaigned to send home three million immigrants, has repeatedly said his party had nothing to do with the attack and complained he was the victim of a witchhunt.
A fifth member of the neo-Nazi group, Jean-Claude Gos, was killed in a motorcycle accident in December 1993. None were members of the National Front.

At the time of their arrests, investigators said all four were either members or sympathisers of the tiny Nationalist French and European Party which became known in the late 1980s in connection with a series of attacks on Arab immigrants.
